analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable standards for immigrant detention, ends for-profit detention facilities, and expands immigration judges' role in custody decisions.
analysis.headline: Introduced Dec. 3, 2025 with 135 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support; it went to two committees and their subcommittees, where no action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Department of Homeland Security to write binding standards for every facility holding detained immigrants, inspected by the department's independent Inspector General with fines for failures and contract termination for repeat failures. It would ban solitary confinement, require quick hearings before an immigration judge with a presumption of release, allow detained children no longer to be held in Immigration and Customs Enforcement facilities, and end contracts with private, for-profit detention companies within three years, replacing them with government-run facilities and community-based supervision.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants in DHS custody, their families, and their lawyers. Detainees would get enforceable living standards, private access to counsel, a legal orientation at every facility, no solitary confinement, a court hearing within days of arrest with a presumption of release, and monthly reviews of their detention. People considered vulnerable, including children under 18, pregnant people, and those who filed workplace claims, could not be detained unless the government proves community supervision is impractical. Families and community groups would benefit from a government case-management program instead of ankle monitors, and taxpayers would gain from fines charged to failing contractors.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires DHS to set binding detention standards for every facility and mandates annual unannounced Inspector General inspections, with public reports; facilities that threaten detainees' health, safety, or rights face fines of at least 10 percent of their contract, and repeat offenders lose their contracts entirely.

Every detained immigrant would get a hearing before an immigration judge within 72 hours of an initial custody decision, with a presumption of release that the government must rebut with clear and convincing evidence, and monthly reviews thereafter.
Solitary confinement would be banned outright in DHS custody, and no one under 18 could be held in an ICE-operated or ICE-contracted facility.
Detained immigrants would keep private, confidential access to lawyers and would be transported to appear in other courts, including family court, rather than losing their cases while locked up.

The bill bans contracts with for-profit detention operators within three years, requires facilities to be owned by the government, and replaces electronic ankle monitoring with community-based case management run by nonprofits or DHS at no cost to the immigrant.

Deaths in custody would require congressional notification within 24 hours and a public investigation with a root-cause analysis within 60 days, and detainees injured by standard violations could sue for damages and injunctive relief.

analysis.who_pays: Private prison and detention companies, including contractors operating ICE beds and electronic monitoring vendors, would lose their federal contracts within three years. Local jails and county governments that rent bed space would lose that revenue. DHS would have to build or run its own facilities and fund community case management, and the government would face more litigation and public reporting duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison firms and jail operators

drawbacks.text: Opponents argue the presumption of release, the end of mandatory detention categories, and limits on using criminal charges as the sole basis for detention would allow people the government considers dangerous to remain in communities while their cases proceed.

Requiring all detention facilities to be government-owned within three years could require major capital spending to build and staff federal facilities, and communities whose economies depend on detention contracts or jail bed-rental income would lose it.
An absolute ban on solitary confinement leaves no isolation option even for a detainee who poses a demonstrated safety risk to others in the facility.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections for detainees are concrete and enforceable, backed by fines, contract termination, FOIA coverage, and a right to sue, which is more than current non-binding detention standards provide. The serious tradeoffs are the cost and disruption of converting to government-owned detention and the dispute over release standards; the release provisions would represent a major shift in who is held, not just how they are held.

outcome.mechanism: It sits with subcommittees of the House Judiciary and Homeland Security committees, both chaired by Republicans, and neither has taken up the bill since it was referred on December 4, 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced Dec. 3, 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, the Homeland Security Committee, splitting it between two panels.
Two days later it was sent to the Border Security and Enforcement subcommittee and the Oversight, Investigations, and Accountability subcommittee, and no further action has been recorded since.
All 135 cosponsors are House Democrats, about 62 percent of the caucus, with no Republican cosponsors listed.

The bill would end for-profit detention contracts within three years and ban electronic ankle monitoring as an alternative to detention, directly affecting companies that hold federal detention and monitoring contracts.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, private detention and monitoring contractors keep operating under existing rules while the bill waits.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on Dec. 3, 2025 and has taken no action since; the bill sits at the Border Security and Enforcement subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: All 135 cosponsors are House Democrats, roughly 62 percent of the 217-member caucus, and no Republican has signed on; the committees that would move the bill are chaired by Republicans.

industries.note: Within three years the bill bans all contracts with for-profit entities that own or operate detention facilities and requires DHS-owned facilities instead, ending the ICE private-detention business. It also imposes fines and contract termination for facilities that fail standards, so companies that profit from holding immigrants see the bill as a direct threat to their revenue.

The bill bans ankle monitors and other electronic surveillance in its alternatives-to-detention program and bars for-profit contracts for detention-related monitoring, cutting off a growing federal revenue stream that charges for tracking immigrants.
The bill phases out the use of jails to hold detained immigrants and requires DHS-owned facilities, eliminating bed-rental income that many county governments count on from ICE.

The bill directs DHS to prioritize direct contracts with community-based nonprofits for case management and requires the Legal Orientation Program to be run by a nonprofit with immigration law expertise at every facility, steering public money to community organizations instead of contractors.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and a House Republican majority controlling both referral committees and the floor calendar, the bill is very likely to die in subcommittee this Congress, as previous versions of the Dignity for Detained Immigrants Act have. Its realistic path to advancement would be as provisions in a larger package, such as an appropriations or DHS authorization bill negotiated after an election changes chamber control.
